facts: Vin de France replaced Vin de Table and allows the grape variety and vintage to be shown on the label.
IGP basically replaced Vin de Pays, and former VDQS wines had to qualify as AOP or be downgraded to IGP.
If a single varietal name is used on a French label, the wine must be made from a minimum of 85% of that variety.
The Vosges mountains shelter Alsace from rain and maritime influence, so the region is rather dry and sunny.
Vendange Tardive (VT) and Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN) have been late harvest designations since 1983, and SGN means grapes affected by noble rot.
Minimum must weights are 235 g/L for Riesling VT and 276 g/L for Riesling SGN, and 257 g/L and 306 g/L for Pinot Gris and Gewürztraminer.
Alsace wine must legally be bottled in tall bottles called flûtes d'Alsace, known in the AOC rules as the vin du Rhin bottle.
Red Beaujolais is made from Gamay, often by semi-carbonic maceration, with whole clusters fermenting in cement or stainless steel tanks, which gives a fruity wine without much tannin.
There are three tiers: Beaujolais AOC, Beaujolais-Villages AOC in the north, and Cru Beaujolais with ten villages or areas.
From north to south the ten crus are Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly.
The Gironde estuary and the Garonne and Dordogne rivers give Bordeaux an Atlantic climate, and the best vineyards sit on well-drained gravel soils near the Gironde.
Château Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth in 1973, and Château d'Yquem is the only superior first growth of Sauternes.
Saint-Émilion was classified in 1955 and is updated about every ten years, Graves in 1953 and 1959, and Pomerol has no official classification.
Burgundy classifications follow geography, not producers, with four levels from regional and village to Premier Cru and Grand Cru.
Delineating vineyards by terroir goes back to medieval times, and the climats of Burgundy are on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
The most famous wines are dry reds from Pinot noir and whites from Chardonnay, with Gamay and Aligoté also grown.
Chablis has four levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru, with Chablis AOC designated in 1938 and Petit Chablis in 1944.
Chablis must be made from Chardonnay alone, and typically shows much less oak influence than the white wines of the rest of Burgundy.
All Grand Cru and Premier Cru vineyards are on Kimmeridgean soil, which gives a mineral, flinty note, while most Petit Chablis is on younger Portlandian soil.
The seven Grand Cru vineyards lie on one southwest-facing hill above the town: Bougros, Les Preuses, Vaudésir, Grenouilles, Valmur, Les Clos and Blanchot.
Spring frost from March to early May is a major risk, and protection includes smudge pots and sprinklers that coat the vines in ice.
Champagne gets its bubbles from a second fermentation in the bottle, and the appellation requires a minimum of fifteen months before release.
Almost all champagne uses Chardonnay, Pinot noir and Pinot meunier, with blanc de blancs made from 100% Chardonnay and blanc de noirs from Pinot noir, Pinot meunier or both.
After ageing, the lees are riddled into the bottle neck, the neck is frozen and disgorged, and a dosage of sugar and wine is added.
Houses may use no more than 80% of a vintage's harvest for vintage champagne, which keeps at least 20% for non-vintage blends.
The rules drawn up in 1923 were the first appellation contrôlée rules in France and the prototype for later AOC rules, and became national law on 15 May 1936.
The original rules allowed ten varieties, amended to thirteen in 1936 and eighteen in 2009, with no split between principal and accessory varieties.
Red and white varieties are allowed in both colours, and most wines are Grenache-led blends, with Grenache noir at 72% of the vineyard in 2004.
In the north and north-east, galets roulés, round pebbles, cover the clay soil, hold the sun's heat and release it at night to speed ripening.
Yields are limited to 35 hl/ha, and wines must reach a minimum of 12.5% alcohol with no chaptalization allowed.
Only about one in 16 bottles produced in the appellation contains white wine.
Reds continue south from the Côte de Nuits but grow lighter and more perfumed, with the great white Burgundies in Meursault and Chassagne-Montrachet farther south.
The Cortons in Aloxe-Corton are the only Grand Cru reds in the district, and Corton-Charlemagne is a great white Grand Cru reaching into Pernand and Ladoix.
The Montrachet Grand Crus are split between Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet and include Chevalier-Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet.
Meursault has no Grand Crus but grows almost only Chardonnay, which makes rich white Burgundy that develops a nutty character with time.
Côte de Beaune Villages is a general appellation for 16 villages, excluding Aloxe-Corton, Pommard, Volnay and Beaune.
Pommard makes some of the most tannic and full-bodied wines of the Côte d'Or, while Volnay is lighter, more elegant and more graceful.
The Côte de Nuits covers fourteen communes, and six of them produce grand cru wines.
There are 24 Grand Cru vineyards clustered around six villages, and more than 100 Premier Cru vineyards across the region.
Since the mid 19th century nearly all Premier and Grand Cru vineyards have been planted entirely to Pinot noir.
Syrah and Viognier are the only permitted grapes, and Côte-Rôtie is red wine from Syrah with up to 20% Viognier.
Under the appellation rules, Syrah and Viognier, if used, must be fermented at the same time, a process known as cofermentation.
The Côte Brune in the north has dark, iron-rich schist, and the Côte Blonde has pale granite and schist soil.
Côte Blonde wines are more balanced, elegant and meant for earlier drinking, while Côte Brune wines have more tannin and age longer.
The name means the roasted slope and refers to the long hours of sun, in a continental climate unlike the more Mediterranean southern Rhône.
The AOC may be used only for red wine with Pinot noir as the main grape variety.
There are nine Grand Cru vineyards, Chambertin and eight others named Chambertin in combination with something else, such as Chapelle-Chambertin.
The nine Grands Crus all lie south of the town, on both sides of the Route des Grands Crus.
Chambertin-Clos de Bèze may also be called Chambertin, and Charmes-Chambertin and Mazoyères-Chambertin share a production zone, so those names are interchangeable.
Twenty-six climats are classified as Premier Cru, and Clos Saint-Jacques is typically the most highly regarded of them.
Graves, meaning gravelly land, lies on the left bank of the Garonne upstream of Bordeaux, and its glacial gravel soils include white quartz deposits.
It is the only Bordeaux subregion famed for reds, dry whites and sweet wines, though red wines dominate production.
Red Graves producers were classified in 1953, and dry whites were added in the updated 1959 classification.
In 1987 the part closest to the city of Bordeaux became a separate AOC, Pessac-Léognan, home of first growth Château Haut-Brion.
Reds are led by Cabernet Sauvignon with somewhat more Merlot than in the Médoc, and dry whites blend Sauvignon blanc and Sémillon.
Graves AOC is the basic appellation for red and dry white wine, and Graves Supérieures AOC is for sweet white wine.
